utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First of all, the Chamber apologises. It was for a small, although urgent, medical reason that we have a delay of 20 minutes starting the case. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm ready, Your Honour, after the Defence concludes its direct examination. I understand they have another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes, that's right. We're not ready yet. So therefore, Mr. Josse, I should have asked you whether you are ready to finish the examination-in-chief of Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Banduka into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Josse will now continue the examination-in-chief. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Josse: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, the first thing I want to ask you about this morning is about the housing of some of the Muslim population of Hadzici in the cultural sports centre. Firstly, did you ever visit that place when it was used in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was running the place when it was used in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security was provided by the police, and the centre, at the moment when it was opened as a protection centre, at the beginning it was the Crisis Staff of the municipality that ran the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was housed there? Which sort of person?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many individuals of different sex and age were accommodated there. Primarily individuals of Muslim ethnicity for whom the Crisis Staff thought that they would be best protected there from anything unpleasant that might occur to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that you received about the facilities within the cultural sports centre came from where or from whom, please?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with that centre before the war, because I spent a lot of time there. This centre was part of the secondary school, and that centre served as the school gymnasium. I know that the centre was constructed in such a way that it had separate toilets for men and for women, and it also had separate dressing-rooms for men and for women. While people were accommodated there, we received some information. The conditions were not too good, but in Hadzici we didn't have either a hotel or a motel or any other sort of accommodation, and that's why we believe that this facility would provide those who stayed there at the time with the best possible conditions. And I would like to add to that one more thing. Food that was provided to those who were in the centre was the same that was provided to everybody else in Hadzici who found refuge there and who came to perform certain duties during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any instance of abuse or the suchlike of the people who were housed in that centre?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of an instance. I believe that this happened in mid-June. We were informed that a certain group of people had stormed, so to say, into that centre, and ill-treated people there, physically abused some of the individuals there, that is to say. At a meeting of the Crisis Staff, we decided that it was something bad that happened at the hand of that group, and that's why we asked members of the police, i.e., the leadership of the police, to remove those people from our midst and to prevent anybody from entering those premises. And I believe that this was done and that this was the only incident of the sort, as far as I know. On the order of the police, I believe that it was even the chief of police who issued a written order. It was forbidden to anybody who did not have the authority to enter the facility to go there. It was only the police that were allowed to enter the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, in view of the evidence the Chamber has received, and before going into any ill-treatment of those who were housed there, can you imagine that the first burning question for the Chamber is a different one, that is, whether those that were housed were free to go or not. I mean, we'd like to know whether this witness is talking about a reception centre or about a detention facility. Wouldn't that be the logical first issue to be explored? Because it remains rather vague this way. And therefore, perhaps it's a matter to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to help the Chamber as to whether the people who were housed in this centre were free to come and go?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they could come in and go out, but I think that the personnel that provided security for the centre had to be consulted. They had to give their approval. The centre was opened in order to protect those individuals after the killings on both sides. There was an imminent danger that somebody else might get killed. In other words, I think that the persons who stayed in the centre could go out, provided that it was approved by the personnel that secured the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask how often such approval was applied for and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the learned Judge's question, Mr. Banduka. Are you able to help with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't provide you with those details, because those are details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're not details, Mr. Banduka. It is in the core of the issue. The core of the issue, whether people were detained there or whether people were protected there. If you say, "I don't know whether they applied for getting out," that means that they could not, on their own, decide to leave that facility. And therefore, it's of -- it's not a detail, but it's the core of the issue whether they actually applied for and could leave the place, or whether they, as a matter of fact, were refused to leave that place. Do you understand that it's not a detail but that it's rather essential? Did you hear anything about it, apart from any -- I'm not asking about Mr. A or Madam B, but did you hear about free movement in or out or considerable restrictions to that freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said details, I meant to say that I wouldn't know how many such cases there were. I believe that the movement of these people was restricted, i.e., those who wanted to get out obviously had to talk to the persons, either the policemen who provided the security for the facility. I don't think that there were any special restrictions because people were accommodated there for their own protection. We even had cases and situations that people came to the municipality and they asked to be accommodated there, because that's where they felt the safest. As of mid-May, or rather, the day from when the centre was opened, there were some sort of exchanges. People expressed a desire to leave and go to the Muslim territory. There were restrictions in one sense, but also there was freedom of movement and freedom to go out of the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, where you said "we even had cases and situations that people came to the municipality and they asked to be accommodated," does that mean that there were other cases, and may I take it from your answer that the other cases were certainly not less frequent that people came there without having applied to be admitted to that centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said it several times. This was a protective measure, primarily. It was an act of protection to provide security for these people. We did not have enough police officers or civilian protection staff who could provide security for literally every house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. It's not an answer to my question. You continue to emphasise the reasons why people were there. My question was whether they were all there because they had asked to be admitted or whether some of them were brought there because your people thought that they would be safer there, and therefore they had to be brought to that place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less, people went there on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does that mean, more or less? To what extent less and to what extent more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in practical terms, when most of one neighbourhood or one village expressed a desire to go there, there were also people who stayed in their homes. However, when a majority left, then either them or we estimated that the minority who had remained would find themselves in dire straits. They would be ill-treated, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To cut it short: There were people who might not have wished to go there, but since you thought it better for their protection, they were forced to join the others in this facility; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Forced" is a very serious term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but they had to join the others; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't have to. Based on some agreements, based on some estimates, assessments, people concluded that they would be safer there. It was more persuasion than anything else. They were more persuaded than being forced to go there, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us that this housing centre, let's call it that way, was set up by the Crisis Staff. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were a member of the Crisis Staff at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When an organisation, whatever it is, takes on the responsibility of setting up a housing or accommodation centre that will accommodate a large number of people, I suppose that this organisation that has set up the centre takes measures in order to check what's going on, how things are going, because this organisation is responsible for the centre it has created. My question is the following: Did you personally try to see how things were developing in the centre? Did you yourself, on your own or with other people, did you go there, or would colleagues from the Crisis Staff regularly go to the housing or accommodation centre in order to see what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course we were informed about the conditions, and I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, but my question was very specific. I was asking you if you ever went there to see how things were going, how things were proceeding there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already answered that, and I said that I never went there. I had some other tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when incidents took place, you told us that men entered there by force and things, that there were problems with people within the centre. The police was ordered to evict these attackers. Did you go there to see what had been going on? Did you go there on the spot? Because a very serious incident had taken place, apparently. Did you go there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't go there. At the time, I may not have even been there. We could not issue orders to the police. It was not the Crisis Staff that controlled the police, and we couldn't issue orders to them. We stated that what had happened was an ugly thing, and that is why we recommended and we requested from the police to prevent any such incidents from happening in the future. We did not have any authority over the police, or, to be more precise, there were very few policemen that provided security for the centre. And as far as I know, the policemen who provided security for the centre could not stand up to that group that broke into the centre, because there were too few of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in your mind, don't you acknowledge that when you set up such an organisation, which is very specific in this background we are all aware with, when you set up such a centre, when you take on the responsibility of setting up such a centre, don't you then have the duty to go there on the spot to monitor, to control what's going on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not the only member of the Crisis Staff, and I couldn't be in a hundred places at the same time. I've already told you that I didn't go to the centre. When this incident happened, my house had already burned down, my family had already been scattered all over the place. I had my personal problems. There was shelling every day. A lot of refugees arrived in Hadzici from Zenica and other parts of Bosnia. You have to appreciate that we could not control every single detail. We couldn't monitor everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question, a very short question. You said you never went there. Do you know of any other member of the Crisis Staff who went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened 13 years ago. Those are tiny details, and I'm afraid I can't remember as I sit here. I suppose somebody did go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's deal firstly with Muslims. People who were suspected of having broken the law, where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first tell you that the police station in Hadzici, which did have a detention unit before the conflict broke out, was damaged, or partly torched, at the beginning of the conflict, and the police had moved out and they found new premises in the municipality building. As far as I know, on the ground floor of the municipality building, there was a makeshift detention unit, and those who had opened fire or had done something that had to be investigated by the police were brought to that detention unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if they were going to be detained for a longer period of time, where did they then go?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For quite some time, nobody was detained. Around the 20th of June, as far as I can remember, all those for whom the police had some information or had done something about them were transferred to the Kula prison, which was a proper prison, in keeping with the laws of the then Republika Srpska. In other words, I think that nobody spent over a month in that detention unit, and under the law, even today, anybody can be kept in custody for up to one month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Josse, but there's a specific item that we find interesting, because this Kula centre has been mentioned several times, and when we review the documents we have here, we can't identify where this Kula centre is located. Can you tell us where it was located? Was it located in your municipality? Was it located in a village of your municipality? Could you give us that information, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Kula prison was not in the territory of our municipality. It is in a different municipality, in the municipality of Ilidza, which is some 20 kilometres away from the Hadzici municipality. It was a prison even in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was provided by the law of the pre-war Bosnia and Herzegovina state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this specification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that subject, Mr. Banduka, am I right the Kula prison is in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we've heard in this Court about the Lukavica barracks. Do you know the distance between the barracks and the prison?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the barracks and the prison, up to two kilometres, I would say. There were two barracks in Lukavica, and the distance from one of them is some two kilometres, and from the other, maybe three kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about prisoners of war? Where were they detained?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What prisoners of war are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to anyone that might have been caught in the course of fighting, or a soldier from the other side, a Muslim soldier, who had surrendered; anything along those lines is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that it was a makeshift detention unit, where people were kept up to the month of June, the 20th of June. This was on the ground floor of the municipality building. And after that, they were transferred to the Kula prison. And later on, as the war progressed, there was no detention in Hadzici. And when it came to the prisoners of war that you're asking me about, it was the matter for the army. I don't know whether the army had some sort of a detention or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Serbs who had been detained by Muslim or Muslim forces, where were they detained?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information and the information that is widely known, in Tarcin, that is in the part of the municipality that was under the control of Muslims, there were three such prisoners or camps, as those people called them. One was a silo in Tarcin, the Krupska Rijeka barracks, in Zovik, and the primary school in Pazarici also served as a prison for a while, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think we can deal with this quite broadly. So far as Silos is concerned, after the war, you have obtained quite a large number of statements from people who were detained there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've said that was in Tarcin, which was in the municipality. What was that building before the war, before it was used as a place of detention of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a storage for wheat. It was huge. I just happened to go there before the war, because this is where we bought [as interpreted] wheat. The silo was split into different parts. I don't know how much wheat it contained. All of these compartments that used to store wheat were emptied and they were turned into cells for prisoners. This camp, or prison, whatever you want to call it, was established on the 11th of May, and the first Serb prisoners were taken there from the territory that was under the control of Muslims. And as I already said during the first day of my testimony, this is where the prisoners for that prison came from, from the territory that was controlled by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information you have just given the Chamber, for example, that the prison was established on the 11th of May in Silos, where does that information come from?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. As I have already said, before the war broke out, we had a line, a separation line that separated the Serbs from the Muslims that I showed you on the map. In the early days of May, people still crossed from one side to the other through various channels. Hadzici borders on the municipality of Kiseljak, which is a predominantly Croat municipality, so from the territory that was under the control of Croats, people could go from one side to another. The Croats acted as mediators in that. And that's where the initial information came from, directly from people who had left Tarcin and Pazarici and arrived in our territory brought news to us about that prison. And the system of exchanges, if I may call it that, started as early as June. Individuals and groups were involved in that, and it was only later that the commissions for exchanges were established. But the exchanges were taking place all throughout the war, and those people who had been exchanged brought fresh information as to what was going on on the other side and what facilities had been put in place and served as prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right that you have brought with you a number of statements from people who were detained in the camp in Tarcin at Silos; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm not going to put them in evidence in this way, Your Honour, but I just want to ask the witness this: A number of these people you knew, a number, at least one or two, were on the list of members of the Municipal Assembly that you showed us last week?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also brought with you a document that relates to prisoner of war exchange in relation to the commission that you've just referred to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence, so to speak, are lucky in relation to this, because the Prosecution had already had this document and had had it properly translated. So though it doesn't appear in Your Honours' bundle, it's about to, and with an official translation, I'm glad to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've got plenty of copies. If they could be handed out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please provide them, and to the witness. Mr. Josse, when you referred to the members of the Municipal Assembly, we have a list of deputies who attended and we have a list of candidates. Which one were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness -- I'll come to that document in a moment. Could the witness have Exhibit D103? Could he also have tab 3, which we haven't yet sought to admit in evidence. I think I will at this point in time, bearing in mind that question. D103, which is tab 1, and tab 3, which is presently unnumbered. It might, Madam Usher, be best if the witness actually had the document in front of him. We've all got copies -- he has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to help us, by reference to that document, as to whom you know was detained, and also from whom you obtained a statement? Two different questions. Perhaps -- sorry. Go ahead, Mr. Banduka. Otherwise I think I can help you.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here on the screen, under 9, Radojka Pandurevic. I got a statement from her. She left the prison in January 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we go to tab 3, please, we see that she is number 18; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's also right, isn't it -- I hope I can be permitted to lead in this way. If we look at number 30 on tab 3, that's Branko Golub from -- he is described as a --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- detainee from another statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And exactly the same position so far as number 39 is concerned, Mr., I assume it is, Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, looking either at tab 1 or tab 3, were any other members of the Municipal Assembly a prisoner, either in the course of fighting or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 1, Milo Bratic, number 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was in the democratic socialist alliance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The League of Communists, the Socialist Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Radmilo Acimovic, number 16, the same. The League of Communists, the Socialist Democratic Party. But Radmilo Acimovic - I'm not sure - he was not there all the time, or rather, I think he was exchanged in 1993, whereas Mr. Bratic, who is under number 13, also spent the entire war in prison. Then, Simo Lalusic, Democratic Socialist Alliance, Union of the Reformist Forces of Yugoslavia, under number 39. Then Sreten Samoukovic, the League of Communists, the Socialist Democratic Party, number 19. That would be about it. That's as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just make this brief observation? Your Honour might recall asking why this one had been printed in full, and Mr. Krajisnik gave some instructions which I didn't repeat at that time. It was, to be fair to Mr. Krajisnik, for this exact reason. Those were the instructions he in fact gave me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But may just ask you,

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this moment, Mr. Josse makes an effort in establishing that a number of members of the Municipal Assembly were detained by Muslims. Is that something which is -- and were detained, some of them, for a very long period of time. Is that contested by the Prosecution, apart from how relevant you consider it to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, aside from the relevance objection, I have no information to dispute this at the present time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if Mr. Josse would have asked the witness whether it's -- whether there were a considerable number of people detained for a longer period of time, would that have caused you to contest that at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it may be clear that apart from the relevance issue, where you said this is mainly background, I do understand that the Prosecution would not seek to undermine a -- I would say a testimony which would have said the same without all of the details. Of course, if it would have been contested, then you would have that list and you could say: Is it true that it's this person, that person, that person. But we now spend a lot of time on finding out whether there was Mr. A, B, C, or Mrs. A, B, C, which might not be of such importance at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't going to ask those questions. I only asked them because Your Honour raised the subject. Your Honour specifically asked the witness to look at the document, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Otherwise I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there was some misunderstanding. It was unclear whether you were referring to tab 3 or tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because neither of these, as a matter of fact, is a list of members of the municipality. One is an attendance list, and of course one could consider those who attended to be members. But it doesn't mean that those who did not attend were not members. And the other one was a candidates list. That's the only reason. But this is a complete misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I thought Your Honour was interested in the point and that's why I then developed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, it was a malcommunication. I just wanted to know whether you referred to tab 1 or to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could tab 3 be given a number, bearing in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly now it needs a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps the witness could now have a look and deal, I think fairly speedily, with the municipal Commission for Exchange of prisoners of war in late 1992. He'll obviously need the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, if you can, Mr. Banduka: What was the commission?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a commission that had been established by the Municipal Assembly for the exchange of detained persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent were you involved in the commission?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very little, or rather, just to the extent to which I attended meetings of the Municipal Assembly, where information was provided about the work of the commission. So that would be it. The amount of information that I received at meetings of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I simply ask that this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next piece of evidence, Your Honour, I'm going to ostensibly lead on it, not dissimilar to what we've heard in one sense, and I suspect it will not be challenged. But if my learned friend takes objection at any point, then no doubt he will stop me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You became a member of a commission for the confirmation of crimes against the Serb population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did that mean? What was your role as a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as we had our first victims, we decided, on the basis of the experience we had, too, from some other wars, or rather, such situations, we established a commission which was supposed to deal with all the facts, or rather, to state which were the crimes that were committed at a given point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your worst personal experience in the course of doing the job was on the 26th of May, when you went to a village called Kasatici; is that correct? Is that right, Mr. Banduka? Yes. I see you nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This village had come under attack the day before and 26 people within the village had been killed?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a small correction. Not all the people were local people. It was a mixed population, and, as I said, on the first day, in a way it was divided. In one part, the Serbs were a majority, and in the other part the Muslims were a majority. It was an all-out attack and there were barracks nearby or rather some lines were already there. There was a total of 25 fatalities. Some were fighters, defenders of the territory, and five local civilians got killed as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw the bodies of some or all of those civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They came from a family called Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two older members of the family who were over 60 had been killed at their doorstep?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I describe this? I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, at that time, the commission was not complete, but there was fear. A woman was supposed to be there, a nurse, a doctor, another lawyer. But most of them, out of fear, did not attend. Having realised that a crime had been committed and that the Muslims had penetrated into that part of the village where these people got killed, we carefully came to the scene and we saw this sight in the yard of the family house. In an area that was about as big as this courtroom, that's how big the yard was, that is where we found four bodies. Dejan Milosevic and Jolanka [phoen] Milosevic, who were old people, they were a married couple, then their son Aco, who was around my age, 40-ish, and the fourth one was Srdjan Milosevic, a close relative of theirs, who was partly retarded too. Namely, his eyesight was not good. They stayed in that part of the village, so that the army, or rather, the Muslim armed forces that came by torched the area and killed the four of them. This is vividly before my eyes, as if I could see it even now. The old woman had been shot in the back. Dejan was lying on his back and the young Srdjan who was hit, had his trousers torn in the genital area, whereas Aco was lying and he held his hands like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me object to this, Your Honour. Again, I come back to the issue of tu quoque, and I ask my learned friend for the relevancy of this information, and particularly in this detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I do understand that this testimony is not presented in the context of tu quoque. At the same time, Mr. Josse, perhaps if we look at the answers and the details of the answers of the witness, of course we should take care that the background is not depicted in more detail as what is on the foreground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I accept Your Honour's observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. We do understand from the testimony of this witness that cruel things happened in a way which shows certainly some similarity - I'm not talking about quantity, but certainly at this moment about quality - where Serbs were victims of atrocities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on to a different topic, one of more general application, Mr. Banduka, the water-supply in Hadzici. Tell the Chamber about that, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. As soon as the war broke out, and I've described that already, for the most part, Hadzici remained without water. Actually, Hadzici got its water from four or five different sources before the war. Since Hadzici is in a valley and the sources of water were actual water sources, they were under Muslim control, most of them, except for one particular water source which was there to supply the technical overhaul institute. And a smaller part of town was on the other side of the river. The rest of the territory of the municipality of Hadzici remained without water, immediately, because the Muslims closed off all supplies, because the water sources were on their side and that's the way it was primarily -- or rather, throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was the water -- how and when was the water restored?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts made, in spite of the war. In 1993 an attempt was made, or rather, there was a meeting arranged through the UNHCR and UNPROFOR. The Muslim and the Serb sides met, and some kind of exchange of civilians was agreed upon then, that is to say, they went from one side to the other. And also what was said was that water and electricity should be made available. I think that there was water only for a day or two, and then it was shut off again. So in 1994, we dug a few wells, four wells, with the assistance of the ODA, an English organisation, and that is the first time we managed to ensure water-supply. Before that, we got water on trucks and in other ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think a British government minister came to visit this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, do we really have to go into -- I mean, we are going into details. I do understand that the witness wants to bring to our attention as a contextual background information that water supplies under the control of the Muslims were manipulated to the expense of the Serbian population and most of the sources of water. If we go into all kind of details, then the Chamber will have to -- I mean, whether it was a British minister or a French minister or a Portuguese minister, whether there were any negotiations meanwhile that failed -- should we have to establish that, whose fault it was that they failed? It's clear that this witness, from his recollection, tells us that there was an unfair treatment of the Serbs by the Muslims in the manipulation of water supplies. That depicts part of the background. I really wonder whether we should go into further detail, because every new piece of information will create the need to clarify issues, et cetera. So therefore, for the time being, perhaps we leave it at that. I didn't want to cut you off when a British minister comes in, so if that is really of relevance, Mr. Josse, please present your British minister and then we'll move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Could I just say, if Your Honour re-makes that observation, in general, I will almost invariably move on. So if Your Honours says enough of this to me, I will very rarely stand my ground and argue. I will generally move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it's also an encouragement to seek the moment yourself when a little bit of information -- and you could even talk about it with Mr. Harmon and say: I want to present this and this and this. I'd rather in a very short way to depict part of the background. Would that cause a lot of problems, yes or no? And then you know yourself more or less. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become president of the Executive Committee of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of December, I think, that an Assembly meeting was held, in 1992. So then it was from the 1st of January, 1993 that I held the position, all the way up to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you now to have a look, please, at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour. It's a Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've had an opportunity to read this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Again we're going into testimony at this juncture that is not identified on the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse. Or would you consider it a rule of customary law that the document A and B document will be presented to any witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will present it to virtually every witness I call. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We experience that very often. It doesn't take much time, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but in terms of the facts that the witness is going to provide in respect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It should be provided to the Prosecutor, pursuant to Rule 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, would you please include in your 65 ter summaries in the future mainly what you expect the witness to testify about in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us at all with any observations or evidence about that document?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have nothing to say, no observations to make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll have it back.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the document is dated the 19th of December, 1991, and at the end I see the Crisis Staff. No, I mean really, I am not aware of the existence of the Crisis Staff in December 1991. I don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll have it back. Thank you. As far as you are aware, did Mr. Krajisnik come to Hadzici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with Mr. Krajisnik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I and Mr. Lubura, who was also a member of the Crisis Staff - I think it was the month of June - we paid a visit to the wounded in the hospital at Sokolac in Pale, and that's when we stopped by at the meeting where the gentlemen of the Presidency were, and we saw Biljana Plavsic a bit, and then, separately, Mr. Krajisnik too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened at the meeting with Mr. Krajisnik? What was said? What was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said. We had already gone as some kind of representatives to visit our wounded, and there were a lot of them. And we simply took that opportunity to stop by, to get some information about the general situation, and to talk a bit about everything, or rather, about what was going on in Hadzici, what kind of situation we were facing, how we lived. It was sort of - how should I put this - a discussion at a humane level, between us who were staying in Hadzici at the time, and that was part of Sarajevsko Polje, Hadzici, Ilijas, Vogosca, Rajlovac, even before the war, and we were cut off from the rest of Republika Srpska. We didn't have any proper communication. In order to reach Pale we had to take forest paths, village paths and they were constantly under fire, right? So we went through an area that was very difficult to negotiate. So we wanted to have this talk, and in addition to that, Mr. Krajisnik is from that area, so it was the right thing to do. It is what any human being would have done, to stop by and have a chat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, I want to ask you this: You've already told the Chamber that you left Hadzici after the Dayton Agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand was the position Mr. Krajisnik was taking at that time in relation to whether Serbs should leave the Sarajevo area following that agreement?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal belief is that Mr. Krajisnik sincerely wanted and strived as much as was under our authority for us to stay in Hadzici, not to leave it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that manifest itself, if at all? In other words, why is it that you say that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, and I'm either fortunate or misfortunate to testify today, at the anniversary of the Dayton Accord, although we did not have electricity in Hadzici at the time, we only learnt one day later what had happened in Dayton. After that we would meet frequently with the leadership or the government, with Mr. Krajisnik. Those meetings would take place in Vogosca and we would analyse the situation. And at all those meetings Mr. Krajisnik was in favour of us staying, of people not leaving. At those meetings, certain conclusions were arrived at. Even the police checkpoints were put up in order to prevent people from leaving, not physically prevent them from leaving but to prevent the floodgate being opened to people leaving. As you know, ugly things happened, and all of his efforts were to that effect. During that period of time, from the Dayton Accords until the moment we left on the 6th of March, Mr. Krajisnik spent some time in Hadzici, and he was in the hall at a meeting which was attended by some three or four thousand people. And his concept was for us to stay. However, this had already taken off the ground. The resettlement was under way, and the first people who left Hadzici were the ones who had found refuge in Hadzici. We had some 5.000 people from Zenica, and as you know, about 15.000 Serbs had moved out from Zenica. They were the first ones to start leaving and the others followed suit and after that it was very difficult to put a stop to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this would be a suitable time for a break. We'll adjourn until 11.00. Mr. Banduka, after the break, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Harmon, to cross-examine the witness, the issue with the videos, has that been resolved? I did understand that -- of course, we have not seen the videos, but that they might be fit to be introduced as contextual exhibits. Is there any further information about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I did in fact e-mail over the weekend one of Your Honour's legal officers, as a courtesy more than anything else. But could I tell the Court this: Though I personally haven't viewed either video, they have been viewed by a member of our team. One of them we would in due course like to adduce in evidence in some way. The e-mail to the legal officer was an inquiry as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've seen that e-mail. So I do understand that you are still in the process of determining whether and to what extent this one video would be appropriate to tender as an exhibit, not introduced through the witness itself. And I take it that then Mr. Harmon will have an opportunity to look at it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course he will, and I was about to say I hasn't as yet had that opportunity. I was about to emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That means that of course the determination now -- it means once the witness has returned, the chance to recall him for those purposes might be small. So it's up to you at this moment to have a closer look at what kind of material is on that video. If it's something the witness has any first-hand, personal knowledge and if you find it important enough, then of course it would be a bad idea to present it as a contextual exhibit. If, however, it's really context rather than direct knowledge of the witness, then we could proceed along the road you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware of that. I mean, broadly speaking, that was the instruction I gave to the staff member who viewed the video. Having said that, I take responsibility for any decision that they make, because ultimately it's my responsibility, not theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course I do understand. Then, Mr. Harmon, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, good morning. Mr. Banduka, you testified that you left the municipality of Hadzici after Dayton and you went to Bratunac, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You became -- did you not become the president of the Presidency in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Presidency? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become the chairman of the SDS Municipal Board after Miroslav Deronjic withdrew his candidacy?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier that you were in the army from July of 1992 until December of 1992. In which unit did you serve? What was the name of your unit?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion of the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander for moral guidance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about what that entails.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entails that, as the assistant commander for moral guidance, you had to look after the morale of the troops, the way they are informed, the access they have to information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had to inform them, did you not, about the policies and the -- of the Republika Srpska; you had to inform them of the actions that were being planned in order to ensure that they fulfilled the objectives of the Republika Srpska leadership; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as such, you had to inform them, as a result of information you received from higher levels, what were the objectives of the -- the strategic objectives of the army that they were attempting to achieve; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. We had very bad communication with the leadership of Republika Srpska, bad in technical terms, I mean. The communication was very often interrupted. It was very difficult for us to physically go to Pale, to the headquarters --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you a question about communications. We'll get to that in due course, Mr. Banduka. My question to you was: You had to inform your people in your units of information that was received from higher levels, including the strategic objectives that the army was attempting to achieve; wasn't that part of your duty and responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the case if we had been a professional army the way you see it. We were a defence army, the army that protected their homes. The army in this case never spoke about any strategic goals. I was more in charge of introducing some order and boost morale of the troops. That's the way we call it, to boost morale. There was a lot of fear. We were completely encircled. Our goal was to defend our homes and to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were unaware, in 1992, of what the objectives were of the political leadership in the Republika Srpska? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what political objectives you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the objectives of -- that were enunciated on the 12th of May, 1992, in the Assembly of the Bosnian Serbs, in which a number of objectives were enunciated, the first of which was the separation of the Muslims from the other peoples, Muslims and Croats from the other -- from the Serbs. Were you unaware of that objective, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not unaware -- you were aware of the objective, then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, and I'm not aware of the details that you are mentioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll change the subject, Mr. Banduka. Let's talk about the Defence Council that you testified to in your previous testimony. It's found -- the evidence is found at page 28 of the LiveNote. You testified that following the multi-party elections, Hadzici had a Municipal Assembly that functioned, and you mentioned a group called the council for National Defence. And I'd like to show you the first exhibit. It is found in tab 1 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it got a number already?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, what I'm showing you, and I'd like to direct your attention to, the document in front of you is Articles 68 and 69, and this is an excerpt from the Law on All People's Defence from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This refers to a Council for national Defence. And my question is: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before you put a question to the witness, my list tells you that it would be Prosecution Exhibit 64, which is a complex exhibit with a lot of tab numbers, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please find out soon what binder, what tab, in P64 it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, was the Council for National Defence that you referred to, which was the only functioning body up until mid-April of 1992, was it a body that was based on this legislation? In other words, did the Municipal Assembly of Hadzici create a Council for National Defence, as required by the law, Article 68?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: While the Assembly was still operational or, as I've said, it was operational up until October, up to the moment when the SDS members attended those meetings, this council did not exist. It was established after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you can put that exhibit aside, Mr. Banduka. Who participated from the Bosnian Serb side in what you referred to as the Council for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ratko Radic participate in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, given the fact that this council was not established by the Assembly in a procedure that was provided for by the law that you have just quoted from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any of those meetings of the Council for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to try to refresh your recollection. Did you attend a meeting with Muslim representatives, Mr. Banduka, where the main issue that was under discussion was the issue of the division of the police force with the Muslims taking the position that the police force should remain multi-ethnic and the Serbs insisting on dividing the police force? Did you attend such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend some meetings. I don't remember whether I attended this particular one. There was some civic council composed of different people, different political options, and we talked about restoring order, calming the situation, and things like that. I don't remember whether I attended this particular meeting that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you participated in some meetings with the civic council, composed of different people, were those different people members of the SDS and members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of both. The term "civic" means that representatives of all political options were represented in it. People who enjoyed reputation, who were not members of any party, who were not members of the Assembly, only respectable people, people who were held in high esteem, who were prominent people in society, they attended those meetings and they were members of this council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many such meetings did you personally attend, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. Such meetings were held quite often on the eve of some conflicts. Then they would be interrupted and then continued. It was the time of confusion, and it is very difficult for me to say, as I sit here, how many of such meetings I attended at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the content of some of those meetings, Mr. Banduka. At some of those meetings, did representatives of the SDS party assert that they did not want to be part of Alija Izetbegovic's state and that they wanted to separate, if necessary, from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can tell you that I never uttered such words when I attended those meetings. I believe that harsh words were said on both sides, and especially when there was this misunderstanding about the reserve force of the police, as I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it ever asserted in your presence that the Muslims -- that the Serbs did not want to be part of a state led by Alija Izetbegovic and that the Serbs wanted to separate, if necessary? Was it ever asserted in your presence, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear such similar words expressed prior to the outset of the war by any political leader, whether in Hadzici or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's change the topic. In your testimony, Mr. Banduka, you testified about the arming of the Muslims, and specifically, you said that the Muslims - and I'm referring to pages 26 and 27 of the LiveNote - you said that the Muslims essentially armed themselves by making a forced entry into the Zunovnica complex and stealing weapons, and that's essentially how they armed themselves. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and this was just one of the ways they armed themselves. This is what I said when we were talking about the barracks in Zunovnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about how the Serbs in your municipality armed themselves and how the Serbs in the adjacent municipalities, Ilidza and Ilijas and other municipalities, armed themselves. They armed themselves, did they not, Mr. Banduka, prior to the commencement of the war in Hadzici, through the assistance of the JNA and through your political party, the SDS? Isn't that how they armed themselves?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS did not have any arms at their disposal. How were they supposed to arm anybody? The way you put it is as if we had an arms depot from which we could arm people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next exhibit, if we can, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The document is P51, Your Honour. It's found in tab 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, I'm going to ask you to take a look at this document and I'm going to direct your attention to a certain part of the document. Mr. Banduka, this is a document. For your information, it's a military secret. It's identified as a top secret. Its conclusions from March of 1992 on the situation in the 2nd Military District area of responsibility. The author of this document is General Kukanjac. And I'd like to direct your attention, Mr. Banduka, to page 4 of the Bosnian version, sub-part 5. It's at the bottom. It says: "Volunteer units in the area of the 2nd Military District." I'd like you to cast your eye, please, on that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That section, Your Honour, is found at page 5 of the English version, at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Page 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 4 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'd like you to read through sub-part (g), Mr. Banduka, on page 5. Mr. Banduka, this report, which is a top secret from General Kukanjac, relates that there are volunteer units in his district, that they have been formed into companies, detachments and battalions, that they total 69.189 people and if you go to sub-part F of this document, you will see that General Kuk's reports to his higher command that the JNA has distributed 51.900 pieces of weapons, 75 per cent, and the SDS, 17.298 pieces. Now, Mr. Banduka, that's what was happening in your municipality, a municipality that had arms depots controlled by the JNA. The SDS was -- and the JNA were distributing weapons to Serbs your municipality before the outbreak of the conflict; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see our municipality here. I see Kalinovik, Foca, Cajnice, and Gorazde. Where did you find our municipality here? And I can see that 300 rifles were distributed in Sarajevo to retired officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can turn to tab 4, Your Honour. If the witness can be directed to tab 4. This needs a new number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 4 has no number yet from -- according to your list, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. It has no number and that's why I'm asking that it be given an exhibit number. I'm sorry. Tab 3, Your Honour. I made a mistake. It's tab 3. Tab 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since by mistake tab 1 was assigned 1001, but had a number already, now tab 4 -- tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab -- oh, you said tab 3, yes, is now --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I direct your attention, Your Honours, for first of all a comparison of this document, because you will see a figure at the end of the column on the right-hand side, 69.198, which matches with the report from General Kukanjac, a figure that he identifies in sub-part B of his report. And you will see at the bottom there's handwriting that is scratched out. And on the English translation, you will, in comparing what has been scratched out, if you make a comparison to sub-part (g) of that report, it's our submission that this is one of the attachments that came from the Kukanjac report. And, Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, if you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 1001, under sub-part 9, you will see that the figure of 1.500 men is identified in Prosecution Exhibit 1001. Do you see that figure?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is item number 9, on the left-hand side. You'll see Hadzici is identified and you'll see the figure of 1.500. Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Banduka, about Serbs in your municipality who were provided weapons by the JNA and by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen Mr. Kukanjac in my life. I've never met him. I have not had an opportunity to do that. And I don't know what this is, what this figure tells you. 1.500 people. I don't understand. What is the essence of this? I don't see it in this document, that is. I can see municipality people, I can see ordinal number and Hadzici and the number of people, 1.500.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the Serbs get their weapons before the war? Where did the Serb people in your municipality get their weapons?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First through the reserve police. Whoever went to the reserve police got weapons. Whoever was a reservist of the JNA got weapons. Whoever was a member of the Territorial Defence got weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence weapons were ordered to be turned in to the JNA by an earlier order issued at the republic level; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the Territorial Defence weapons were turned in to the JNA, does that mean that the JNA was supplying weapons to Serbs who were in the Territorial Defence before the war?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if a person was in the Territorial Defence, then he'd have to get a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, listen to my question, Mr. Banduka. The Territorial Defence members had to turn in their weapons pursuant to an order that was issued at the republic level; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about that? When you say "probably," you seem to hesitate. You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that this order did exist about weapons. Now, was it weapons that were issued to individual members or were these surplus weapons? That was all placed under JNA control. I remember that. But these details, I mean, you put a question as if I were in the JNA or in some kind of staff, as if I was supposed to know all these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, if there's something you don't know, you just tell us. Okay? And even although Mr. Harmon is entitled to verify your answer on whether you really didn't know, then everyone will accept lack of knowledge as your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to tab 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Harmon, could the Chamber be informed -- I'm a bit puzzled about 1001. It seems that these are two lists which very much look like the same, although with different ERN numbers, but handwriting which is not exactly the same. If I look at the 25 at the top, that's a bit different. The typed-out portions seem to be the same. Part of the handwriting in the first -- at the bottom has disappeared. We get a translation of it, which seems to reflect only one of the documents, but I'm not -- yes, because on both of them is handwriting at the bottom, but one of the translations doesn't say anything about the entry. So I wonder first of all where it comes from, and second, why we have the two very much similar copies in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first copy you have, with no translation, it simply wasn't translated, and so perhaps there's a copy that is in your set that is inserted erroneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, we have two translations. I see. Let's just -- let's just go through this tab, then. Tab 3 we're talking about. On the bottom of the first page it says "1 of 5," and the second says "2 of 5," and no handwriting at the bottom of the document is translated. Then I come to 3 of 5, English translation has all the same ERN number. Then we come to 4 of 5, which translates a stricken-out handwriting at the bottom. Then 5 of 5 is empty. And then the two originals are not exactly the same, but both of them have handwriting at the bottom, one, the second one, more complete, because the copy seems to be covering also a tiny little bit at the right-hand side. And I noticed that the handwritten 25 at the top is not exactly the same on the second original as it is on the first one. So quite a lot of puzzles. I'm not asking you to immediately resolve them, but could you please inform us after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the, of course, the next question was: Where do they come from? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They come from the Sarajevo collection, the 2nd Army District offices. That's where they come from. I've just been handed a note informing me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it, then, that it's especially on the basis of the numerical similarity of this 69.198 and the number mentioned in the Kukanjac report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the text at the bottom relates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the 300 Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- to (g), and Your Honour, and you'll see in the last page of the English, page 11, you'll see there were a number of enclosures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it's our submission, Your Honour, that this is one of the enclosures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not looked at page 11 yet. To be quite honest, it stops at -- no, no. It stops at 10, as far as I'm concerned. But attachments on page 10 says 1, 2, and, number 3, text and map. So the position -- we have to understand this to be that this list is one of the attachments to the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. The numbers we have before each town or each city, in the translated version of the text, do not correspond to the original, apparently. What does it mean? Was there an error in the translation? 58, for example, Celinac, in the translation it's 57, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be that there are two 12s on one of the lists, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me try and resolve the various mysteries associated with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in the second translation you find on the 12th Kalinovik and Konjic, and both originals we have only one 12, so I take it that the mistake starts there. Yes. Okay. That's -- well, to some extent we have, it seems, that we have understood already where the mistakes are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the document that is the basis of the military secret conclusions you introduced earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The document that supports the conclusions that I've advanced are found in the text of Prosecution Exhibit 51, and sub-part, and 5 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, let me show you the next exhibit, which is Prosecution Exhibit number 4 -- tab 4, I should say, and it needs a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I get a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 4 would be P1002, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, P1002 is a handwritten document dated the 4th of November -- April the 4th -- April the 11th, 1992. It has a list of people, and at the upper left-hand side it says "advisory organ of the Hadzici Serb Municipal Assembly." It lists your name as number 12, and number 19 it has a man by the name of T. Glavas. Does that list that is before you accurately represent the members of the advisory organ of the Hadzici Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn to the last page of the B/C/S -- I'm sorry, the page that has Y0045809 at the top, you will see your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The reference I'm going to be referring Your Honours to is at the bottom of page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, according to this document, on the 11th of April, 1992, you say, and I quote: "The Serbian TO is already being organised into military units and there is cooperation with the units." And then it's illegible. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before we continue, I'd like you to be very precise in putting these questions to the witness. This witness is called in accordance with his evidence Vidomir Banduka; is that correct? On the list of those who attend, I see a Veljko Banduka, under 2, and I see a Vido Banduka under 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I acknowledge there is an error on my part. You're correct. So let me ask the question differently, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but please be very precise on these kind of matters, because it would be unfair both to the accused and to the witness to put the question the way you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
