utterances.text: Mr. Veljko Banduka asserts in this document that the Serbian TO is already being organised into military units and there is cooperation with the units. What can you tell us about the Serbian TO being organised into military units on April the 11th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what Mr. Veljko Banduka says - that's a completely different person - but let me explain this. My name is Vidomir Banduka. A lot of people called me Vido. So some place it says Vido and some places it says Vidomir because a lot of people called me Vido. Veljko Banduka was a reserve officer, or rather, a reserve -- a JNA reservist, rather, as people said before the war. And, as I've already said, at the meeting of the 11th of April, when we passed a decision to constitute the Assembly, let me not repeat myself, but we also passed a decision to establish the Serb Territorial Defence. Now, what Veljko Banduka meant by this, that there were already organised Serb TO units, I cannot say. I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's continue, then, Mr. Banduka, about the issue of the arming of the Serbian people in your municipality and in adjacent municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next document, Your Honour, which is found at tab 5. This is already an exhibit. It is Nilsson tab 4 and also Prosecution 825, tab 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, this is a document that is dated the 20th of September, 1993. It is addressed to the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs. It is from the Serbian public security station in Ilidza. Its author is Tihomir Glavas, who was, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Banduka, the same Mr. Glavas who was on the advisory committee to the Hadzici Municipal Assembly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you -- I'd like to direct your attention, Mr. Banduka, to the B/C/S version. If you would turn to page 2 of the B/C/S version, the second complete paragraph, starting at Pocetkom 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm referring Your Honours to the bottom of the English version, page 2, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document, Mr. Banduka, read, if you would, please, the paragraph yourself dealing with Pocetkom 1991 and the ensuing paragraph, Dana 05/03/1992, please. Mr. Banduka, this document, from Mr. Glavas, says that at the beginning of 1991, there was a realisation of war as an option for the realisation of national interest, and in order to prepare, there was intense activity undertaken to arm the citizens of Serb nationality and that arms were transported from a variety of locations, including Hadzici, including JNA barracks, and it also, in the next paragraph, refers to a MUP storage in -- it says Dugi, in Potok, which is incorrect, it should say Donje Potok, which was blocked, and the arms and ammunition were distributed to the Serbian people. Does that refresh your recollection about how the Serb people received their arms in your municipality prior to the commencement of the war?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, now you call this a report, don't you, or some kind of information, that was written by a policeman. I'm not a policeman. I did not deal with such things, and I'm not going into that, what the police says and what they did. I did not have much occasion to receive information about what the police does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, you were asked whether, having read this portion, whether it refreshes your memory. That means that after having read it, that something comes into your mind that was not in your mind before. At this moment, no one asked you to comment on knowledge on police reports. Having read this, does this change anything from what you said before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, staying with that same document, I'd like to direct your attention to page 6 of the B/C/S version of the document. If you'd direct your attention there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the English version it is page 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see, Mr. Banduka, a series of names, and Tomislav Kovac. If you'd read very briefly Mr. Kovac's summary. If you'd read the summary in"Sreto Samrdzija," number 8, and if you'd read the summary in Radoslav Tomic, number 11. Do you see those names in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could assist the witness in locating those names. Again, page 6 of the B/C/S version has Mr. Kovac, page 7 has Sreto whose name I cannot pronounce properly, and page 8 was Radoslav Tomic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Tomislav Kovac?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He became the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you invited the witness to read the summaries 1, 8, and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd very much like you first to verify whether the witness had the opportunity to read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll be glad to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read items 1, 8, and 11?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1, 8 -- I've read about Tomislav Kovac, but I don't know these other people. Tomislav Kovac is the only one I knew out of all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're first of all invited to read them. So would you also read the summary of Sreto Samrdzija and then Tomic, Radoslav.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The summaries in respect of each of these gentlemen refers to their work of arming the Serbian people. Does -- you said you knew Mr. Kovac. Did you have contact with him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything in these summaries that assists you in recalling the arming of Serbian people in 1992 in the Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislav Kovac did not live in the municipality of Hadzici, and these two other persons are not from Hadzici. So I don't see how anything can assist me in recalling anybody. I just knew Tomislav Kovac from before the war, when we were both students.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think we've concluded with that topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'd like to add to that, Mr. Banduka, that even if someone is not living in the area, he might write down observations which might assist you in refreshing your memory. So therefore, I'd rather hear whether it does or not, and whether it could have done. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's change -- I'm finished with that document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's change the topic and talk about your testimony that the war in Hadzici started on the 11th of May, 1992. That testimony is found in the LiveNote at page 43. That's where it starts, Your Honours. Let's be perfectly clear, Mr. Banduka. The war in Bosnia had already started before the 11th of May, 1992, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, 1992, in Bijeljina, Arkan had gone into Bijeljina and had forcibly removed Muslims from that municipality. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bijeljina is 200 kilometres away from the place where I lived. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, again, the question was whether you were aware of that. I sometimes am aware of something that happens at a distance of 200 kilometres. So would you please answer the questions and the logic -- if we need further information for that, I'm certain that Mr. Harmon will ask you for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Banduka, on the 8th of April, Arkan attacked Zvornik and the Muslims were forcibly removed from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent to which I could see this on television, that is the degree of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that in April, early April, a war had started in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I was in Sarajevo was on 25 April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you when the last time you were in Sarajevo. I asked you whether you were aware that a war had started in Sarajevo in April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of conflicts. I don't know what you mean when you say "war."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that members of the Hadzici police department, public security station, were fighting in Ilijas in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Banduka, that Muslims were being forced to move out of Ilidza, the municipality that you say was 20 kilometres away from you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of April, Muslims attacked Ilidza and some Serbs got killed. I don't know whether they were forcibly moved or not. Ilidza was divided in the same way Hadzici was divided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could go back to the document that is found at tab 5, Your Honours, the Prosecution Exhibit 825, tab 5. Mr. Banduka, I'd like to direct your attention, Mr. Banduka, to portions of Mr. Glavas's document dealing first of all in the B/C/S the first paragraph at the top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I'm referring to page 2, the penultimate paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to read that paragraph, Mr. Banduka, that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This paragraph says: "Repressive measures undertaken against them," referring to detained Muslims, "for various reasons resulted in them increasingly fleeing and moving out of this municipality." What kind of repressive measures are you aware of that were applied to the Muslims in the municipality adjacent to you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a different municipality. How should I know what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look, then, at the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, just if you would allow me one comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to a paragraph in which "detained Muslims" are mentioned. We heard quite some evidence of this witness this morning on prisons and detentions, where it remained rather unclear what the detention was for. And therefore I invite you, and it's an invitation to Mr. Josse as well, that whenever we are talking about detention situations, that we'd clearly distinguish between prisoners of war being detained, the population of the detained persons, whether any women or children were included. Because otherwise it's -- it would come down to a lot of guessing whether it's Prosecution questions or Defence questions, it's exactly the same, to properly assess the importance of such evidence, we should know what type of detention, what detained population we're talking about, not only ethnicity, although ethnicity, of course, might be of vital importance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I didn't explore that further, Your Honour. This is from the municipality of Ilidza and the witness professes to know nothing of what was going on in the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, let me refer you to page 4 of that very same document in B/C/S, the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, reference is on page 3, the paragraph in the middle of the page in English that starts with the words "general attack on all defence lines."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, read that to yourself and tell me when you've finished reading that, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you finished? You asked me how you should know --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You wanted me to read just this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you asked me a minute ago how you should be aware of anything that was happening in Hadzici, and this document from Mr. Glavas reports that members of the Hadzici police public security station were fighting in Ilidza on April 22nd. Did you have any contacts with those members of the police station who had gone into combat in the municipality adjacent to you? And if so, did they tell you what was happening in the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On that day I was in my village, and we were sowing potato on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the fighting that was taking place in Sarajevo. Let's, in fact, turn to the next exhibit, which is tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It needs a report -- it needs an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 6 would be P1003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, this is a document that is relatively short. If you would cast your eye on this, this is a document that's dated the 4th of May, 1992. It is a daily report from the minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is signed by Mico Stanisic, who is the minister of the interior. This is a document that describes fighting that was going on in the municipality of Sarajevo, Mr. Banduka. It talks about attacks in Ilidza. In the second paragraph it talks about fierce fighting is in progress in Vogosca. The third paragraph, heavy fighting is in progress in Ilijas. In the next paragraph, it says: "The Serbian forces managed to liberate parts of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo." Two paragraphs down it talks about the Serbian forces successfully advancing in fighting in downtown Sarajevo. In fact, this fairly accurately reports information, Mr. Banduka, that Sarajevo, all around you, all around your municipality, was the subject of heavy fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct that the report says that or correct that that is true?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose question am I supposed to answer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon asked you whether it is true that Sarajevo, all around you, all around your municipality, was the subject of heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next exhibit, which is tab number 7. It has already an exhibit number. It's P825, tab 2. Again, this document -- I'd like to show you this document because it refers to fighting that's taking place in Sarajevo, again based on a report of the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. It's dated the 8th of May. Obviously, Mr. Stanisic is preparing reports based on information that he's receiving from the field. And in the second paragraph it talks about "the Serb forces are mopping up Dobrinja neighbourhood, liberating it, and placing this particular part of town under their control." It talks about, on the paragraph -- two paragraphs down, Mr. Banduka, "The Serbian forces have maintained firm control of the positions captured all around town." And in the penultimate paragraph: "The Serbian forces are in full control of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza." Now, Mr. Banduka, the reason I bring these facts to your attention and ask you if you can verify those is because of your evidence that you gave last week that the Muslims from Hadzici left Hadzici as part of a plan. Part of the plan was to evacuate Hadzici before an attack started. And I want to put to you this question: Mr. Banduka, there was a war going on that was all around the Muslims before the 11th of May, 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not a true war. In my view, the way I see war, this was not a war. You're talking about Dobrinja here. Dobrinja was in the hands of Muslims throughout the war. Only two blocks were in the hands of Serbs. You're talking -- actually, he is talking about some other conquest here. I won't go into that. You keep asking me things that I don't know anything about. I lived in Hadzici. On the 8th of May, as I've already told you, I was in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were conflicts, there were clashes, absolutely, in the territory of Sarajevo, as is stated here and as you assert. On the 22nd of April, Ilidza was attacked. Maybe that is what is referred to here. Sarajevo is a huge town, with 500.000 inhabitants. How am I supposed to know what is happening in every corner of that big town? Everybody knew that there were clashes and conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to focus on your opinion, Mr. Banduka, that the reason the Muslims left Hadzici was because there was a plan for them to leave, and after they successfully evacuated Hadzici, Hadzici was attacked. What can you tell us, Mr. Banduka, about an ultimatum that was issued by the SDS to Muslim representatives on the 7th of May to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this ultimatum, and I have repeated so many times already. On the 6th and 7th of May I was in my house. It was St. George's Day, which is my name day, and I had a party. And how can somebody who is not as strong in numbers issue an ultimatum to a more numerous party? Can I explain that, please [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Let me ask the questions and if you feel it necessary, Mr. Josse, he will ask you some questions about that. In fact, Mr. Banduka, on the 9th of May, 1992, there were already clashes in the city of Hadzici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, minor clashes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct -- I'd like to turn to tab 9, Your Honours. If I could turn to tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before doing so, Mr. Harmon, one of the answers of the witness was not entirely clear. You were asked, Mr. Banduka, about an ultimatum issued by the SDS to Muslim representatives on the 7th of May to leave the municipality. Then you said: "I don't know anything about this ultimatum." And then two lines later you said: "And how can somebody who is not as strong in numbers issue an ultimatum to a more numerous party? Can I explain that, please," says the translation. Would you like to explain that, or is it a mistranslation, and were you asking for someone else to explain it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wanted somebody else to explain this to me, and it is only my logic which tells me that it doesn't make sense for somebody who is weaker to issue an ultimatum to somebody who is stronger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, as I said, if logic is really a point, then you'll be specifically asked about it, but here it seems to be a translation issue. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm turning to tab 8, Your Honours, please. If I could get a number for tab 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 8, Your Honours, will be P1004.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, again, I'd like to direct -- this is a document again from Mico Stanisic, and it is dated the 9th of May, 1992. It's an overview of the daily events. And I'd like to direct your attention, Mr. Banduka, to the second paragraph and the third paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, since -- I'd like to direct Your Honours' attention to the second, essentially, bullet point on page 1, and the third bullet point at the bottom, that carries over to page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Banduka, the second -- the first paragraph that I directed you to describes ferocious fighting in the Serb municipality of Ilijas, and the third paragraph describes the fighting that took place in Hadzici, in which the attack is described as ferocious, and it describes no losses from the Serb side but significant losses on the Muslim side. Now, Mr. Banduka, this report of these activities is on the 9th of May. You weren't in Hadzici on the 9th of May. You've told us that you were in your house. Did you hear the shooting that was taking place in Hadzici on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in my village, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the shooting that was taking place on the 9th of May in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was frequent shooting at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there was also an ongoing battle in Hadzici on the 9th, the 10th, and the 11th of May, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next exhibit, which is tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That also needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1005, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Banduka, let me direct your attention in tab 9 to the second paragraph, the second marked paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm referring to the second paragraph on page 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cast an eye on that and read that, please. This is another report on the daily events from the Ministry of the Interior, from Mr. Stanisic, and it describes, Mr. Banduka, heavy fighting that has taken place for the past two days in the Hadzici area, which is referring to the two days before the date of this report. And it describes the situation in Hadzici, "very difficult." Now, again, there was heavy fighting, according to Mr. Stanisic's report, that was going on in the Hadzici area at that time. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's take a look at the next exhibit, then. Actually, how were you aware of that, Mr. Banduka? How was it you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you a minute ago whether you were aware there was heavy fighting in Hadzici area, and you said you were aware of that. And my question next to you was: How were you aware of that, Mr. Banduka? By hearing it? By seeing it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it, I heard it. Hadzici is a small area. On the 11th of May, I found myself at a plateau above Hadzici, some three kilometres from the centre, and from there I could see all these elevations points, for example, Tinovo Brdo. I could see it with my naked eye. I could hear shooting. And there was shooting coming from all directions, from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the 11th of May, Mr. Banduka. I'm asking you about the 9th of May, the 10th of May. Were you aware that there was heavy fighting in Hadzici, in the Hadzici area. At the point in time you described you observed Muslim people fleeing from Hadzici. Were you aware that there was heavy fighting going on in Hadzici and in the area of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, there seems to be some confusion. First, the witness was asked, and I think we are talking about a couple of days before the 10th, what he noticed of any ongoing fighting. Then you confronted the witness with this tab 9, I think it is. Is that correct? Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've confronted him with tab 8, which describes heavy fighting on the 9th of May; tab 9, which is dated the 12th, describes heavy fighting for the two days before the 12th, which would be the 10th, the 11th, and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just checking on whether the report of the 12th, going on for the two past days, so that would include either the 10th and the 11th or the 11th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Either one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said: "I'm not asking you about the 11th of May, Mr. Banduka. I'm asking you about the 9th of May, the 10th of May." So that's not entirely clear, in view of the 12th of May, which might well include the 11th as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, it could, but I'm asking him about the 9th and the 10th of May and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So the questions from what you saw are now specifically about the 9th and the 10th, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 9th and 10th I was at home, and as for the fierce fighting on the 9th and 10th, I learnt about that on the 11th. But we could hear shots all the way to my village. On those days, I was in my house, which means I was not where all this fighting was going on. On the 11th of May, there were fierce attacks from all sides. I met with a lot of people and I learnt what had happened on the two or three previous days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood your earlier testimony, Mr. Banduka, that you went out of your house and you met and spoke with the people who were fleeing from Hadzici. Is that correct? You weren't exclusively in your house; you were out of your house for parts of the day, speaking with the people who were fleeing. Did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were out of your house, did you hear combat operations, combat taking place? Did you hear gunshots fired?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, your question is not clear to me. You are referring to my house as some hermetically closed area. Whether I was in the house or in front of the house, I was in my house on the 6th, on the 7th, and on the 8th, which means I was either in the house or around the house. Since there is a road very close to my house on the 7th, 8th, and 9th I saw the columns of people passing through. This was before the real conflict started. Maybe I expressed myself wrongly when I said that the war started on the 11th. This is the date that we consider the beginning of a fully blown conflict. The days that preceded the 11th, I believe that on those days there were skirmishes, incidents, shooting. Nobody got killed. And that is what prompted me and others to say that the 11th can be considered the real beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Banduka, I am a judge. In these last few days I've listened to you, and I thought I'd understood you to say the following: I saw Muslims leaving the town. And you specified that you took this movement of population to be some kind of prior phase before an attack that was about to be launched against the municipality. In fact, part of the population that belonged to a specific group, to the Muslims, left the municipality, and thereafter, they went back, or they turned against the municipality to attack it. This is what I understood you to say yesterday or the day before yesterday, or maybe three days ago. So was this the way you saw the events? Because now, as I listen to you, I have the feeling that this departure of some population could be interpreted differently. It was not a ruse, it was not a trick. They were possibly leaving the town, now, listening to you, because there was heavy fighting. I have a feeling that you gave us a version of events that was somewhat simplified, given the complexity of the situation as it now appears. I mean, you're here to tell us. You are before Judges. You are supposed to be here to tell us what exactly happened then. Now, do you want to go back on what you said and try to tell us what you really saw, what you heard, what you knew then? Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I adhere to my previous statement. On the 11th of May was the beginning of a general attack on Hadzici, and I've already told you that I am also an inhabitant of Hadzici. I was at home, and there was no shooting around my house. The neighbouring village is a Muslim village. In order to get to the centre of Hadzici, I have to pass through a large Muslim village. And the roads were still passable. On the 10th or the 9th of May - I'm not sure - my wife, with my child, went to my sister's place, and my sister lived in Ilidza. And on the 11th I learnt that there had been shooting in Hadzici, as described in this document, and that there were skirmishes between the members of the two police forces. The police station that housed the Muslim police was at the far end of the town, at the exit from Hadzici, leading towards Konjic and Mostar. Maybe you didn't understand me properly. Maybe. When I say that on the 11th of May the war started, I say this because the conflict was much larger and it spread to an area that reached some 10 or 12 kilometres out of the area that had already been controlled by Muslims. And let me say one more thing. The Serbian population that resided in Tarcin and Pazarici, that is, the parts that the Muslims controlled throughout the war, remained in those areas. About 3.000 people remained in those two neighbourhoods. Most of the Muslims that came under the attack on the 9th, 10th, and 11th of May, and a separation line was built through that area, most of the Muslims left that area, and this is where I have drawn my conclusions from, the one that I shared with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask one additional question. The SJB Hadzici, where was that located, the Serb SJB Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the exit from the centre of Hadzici, the residential area stopped; then there was this police station; and this is the road leading from Hadzici towards Konjic and Mostar, towards the area that was under the Muslim control from then onwards. In 1993, this was beyond our lines, the lines where the Serbs had put up their defence lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that within hearing distance from where you lived, loud noises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean where I resided at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance is about 5 kilometres from my house and my village, i.e., my house is in a valley, close to a river. It was rather well sheltered. But you could hear the shots. But there was daily shooting. People fired shots for celebrations, for weddings. Fired shots were not something unusual. Even during the times of peace there was frequent shooting, let alone when the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one of these reports says that "early this morning," and the report dates from the 9th of May, about 0115 hours, "the Serb SJB Hadzici has been attacked by the members of the Muslim paramilitary formations. The attack was ferocious and it was led from all directions toward the station. The members of the Serb SJB Hadzici efficiently responded to the attack while there were no losses in manpower. On the side of the Muslims there were significant losses, several lightly and severely wounded members." Now, this happens in the middle of the night. The way it was described could hardly create any confusion as to whether it was a wedding where a few shots were fired. Did you notice any of this kind which, in the middle of the night, could not be easily, I take it, mistaken from as it is described, "a ferocious attack was led from all directions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What this gentleman describes here, I believe this is just to boost other people's morale. It says here that the Serbian police station came under attack. When you asked me where the public security station was, I told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand you believe that this is just to boost other people's morale, which I understand to be that it's not true what he writes, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comment. The first time I came to the centre of Hadzici - I don't know when it was - between these two police stations that came into conflict, there was a van which served as a barricade. It was shot through. And there were stories saying that the members of the Muslim police had shot at it. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say -- of course you give now a different version of the events, at least something you heard of, and that, therefore, the report, you believe, is just to boost other people's morale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it says here that the Serb side did not suffer any losses and that there were heavy losses on the Muslim side, I don't know how this could be established. I believe that this is an improvisation and this is what I meant when I said that this was to boost the morale of other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The subject of my question was not whether the losses were correctly reflected. It was mainly focussing on a -- what is described as a "ferocious attack from all directions in the middle of the night." And I'm just wondering whether that remained unnoticed to you, if true, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't observe this. It couldn't be heard during the night where I lived. But, according to my subsequent information and according to the stories I heard later on, these were just skirmishes, an occasional shot fired between the two police stations, which were some 200 metres away from each other. This was not a fully blown conflict, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon. Anyway, I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps it would be a better idea to have the break now and to resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The earphones broke that I was about to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, I want to focus your attention on the 11th of May, 1992, when you went up to the top of the hill and when you looked in toward the direction of Hadzici, you said that you saw and heard artillery fire, or fire coming from positions that were held by the Muslims, the positions that were beyond Tinovo Hill. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see or hear any fire coming from positions that -- artillery fire coming from positions that were held by the Serbs, artillery fire that was directed toward the centre of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to the exhibit that is found at tab 10. Could I have a number for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1006, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I direct Your Honours' attention to the first paragraph in tab 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Banduka, I direct your attention in the B/C/S to the first paragraph in that B/C/S document. This is a document again from Minister Stanisic from the Ministry of Interior. It is dated the 11th of May, 1992. Mr. Banduka, tell me when you've finished reviewing that, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, this report, dated the 11th of May, 1992, says that "the Serb forces returned fire on the attacking forces, destroying also with shells the former joint station of the public security in Hadzici, which at the time was held by members of the BH Territorial Defence, the former BH Territorial Defence." Does this report assist you in recalling more clearly the sources of the artillery fire that you observed or saw from the top of the hill where you were looking into Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is referred to here is probably night-time, 0025. I talked about the hill above Hadzici that I reached during the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is -- this refers to -- at least at the beginning, an attack that started at 0025 hours. My question is: Does this assist you in terms of recalling where the artillery fire was coming from, at the time you were looking into Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the gunfire came from above the hill of Tinovo, from the village of Lokve, and also a village that was closer by, and that was Grivici, right next to the technical institute, that was held by the Muslims too. Shells fell right next to me at the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So your answer is that you do not recall any shells coming from Serb-held positions; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during the day or during the night?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 11th of May? Then there was fire coming from Serb positions too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about artillery fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mortar fire, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to go into the next two exhibits. The next two exhibits are for context, Your Honour. They are found at tabs 11 and 12. Tab 11, which I will offer into evidence, is a contextual document. It's an intercept between the Ilidza police station commander, Petko Budisa, and Colonel Gagovic, from the JNA, from the army, and it refers to targeting information, and also refers to APCs and a Praga anti-aircraft gun being in, as it says, "down there," which it's our submission refers to Hadzici. And I'm going to also refer Your Honours again to a contextual document dated May 12th, a conversation again from Ilidza to Colonel Gagovic, again talking about targeting information. My question, Your Honour, is: Should those be given numbers at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If these would be the only ones, the only contextual exhibits, then we would do it, but if you come up with a bundle of contextual exhibits at a later stage, then I think it would be better even to take them out, to return them to you, so that you can use them. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd much rather the latter was done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm satisfied, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir: You mentioned that you were part of a commission which was to investigate crimes committed against Serbs. Why didn't your commission investigate crimes that were committed against Muslims who were members of the Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission had a very short life. I already said that before the 25th, or rather, the 26th, we did what we did, but most of the members of the commission, quite simply, moved on to other jobs. There was a lot of fear involved. Many people were afraid. And I know that very often people would avoid going out to the scenes. So the commission did not have meetings and did not really exist. The intention was exceptionally good, but the situation was such that it was impossible for it to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of the attack on the village of Musici, can you tell the Chamber what happened to all of the Muslim homes that were in the village of Musici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Musici, I was not there. Later on I had the opportunity to pass by that village, and I know that there were damaged houses, destroyed houses, and that probably happened during the conflict. I think it was around the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that all of the Muslim homes after the village was taken over were burned intentionally?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was really all of them, because if there was fighting around that village, and it is important to mention that the village was right next to Mount Igman; it was on the slopes of Mount Igman, that was held by the Muslims. Well, probably in that fighting around the village, many houses were damaged or destroyed, and I witnessed that myself, yes, later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony, sir, you mentioned a battle that took place on the 25th of May, 1992, in the area that was in and around Zunovnica, the Zunovnica conflict, and you said that 25 people had been -- 25 Serbs had been killed in the course of that combat.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Zunovnica complex was a major complex that was a depot that stored ammunition and ordnance and therefore it was a major target, an appropriate target for the other side. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The battle that was -- that you described was a major military battle that took place in Hadzici, in which not only 125 -- 25 Serb soldiers were killed, but approximately 130 Muslim soldiers were killed in their efforts to take over that complex; correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That figure of 130 Muslim soldiers is something that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to offer this without confronting the witness with this, the document that's found in tab 13, just to illuminate further the battle that was described by this witness. And if I could have a number for tab 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It then becomes more or less a contextual exhibit, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll ask him some questions on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that should be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1007, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab 13 of the documents that are before you, sir, you will see that this is in large measure a document that describes the attack that took place on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, description starts in the English on page -- in paragraph 1. It is about the middle of the page, with the paragraph starting "following the situation." And it ends with a description on page 2 of the English, about a third of the way down, where it describes the losses, according to the data that was collected by the Serbs, showing that around 130 men were lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd invite -- I'm sorry. I'd invite the witness to look at all of number 1, if he may, because I've just read the first two paragraphs. They put the rest of the document into context, I'd submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is then invited to read on from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this document, for the record, Your Honour, is a report on the combat readiness of the Serb municipality of Hadzici, delivered to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps operative command, dated the 29th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, does this fairly characterise from the headquarters of the TO headquarters the battle that took place on the 25th and the 26th of May that you related to us in your testimony in direct examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you first ask the witness whether he finished reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thought he had finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you finished reading the document, Mr. Banduka? If not, I'll give you some additional time to read it.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't. It's a very long document. It takes time to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do it, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, does this fairly and accurately describe the battle that you testified about on the 25th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly, it does, but the figures are different. Here it says 15, 20, 9, in respect of the dead, wounded, and missing. I don't think that the figure pertaining to missing persons corresponds to what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than those small details, does this accurately describe the battle that took place on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, yes. What I said earlier on. 130 killed Muslim soldiers, well, that's just an assumption. I know that there were some Muslim casualties, a few remained in this territory, but the figure of 130, I don't know where that comes from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn the topic to something you testified about this morning, and that was the detention of Muslims, or the protection of Muslim civilians at the sports complex. Let me ask you very specifically,

utterances.speaker: MR. BANDUKA
utterances.text: Were there detention facilities in the Hadzici municipality, where Muslim civilians were detained against their will?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already talked about the sports centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were Muslim civilians held against their will in the sports centre?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that we can say yes, but we've already explained that, that it was for the purposes of protection. Quite simply, even then people didn't believe that something could happen to them, something unexpected. So perhaps it's from that point of view that their will was not complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was a Detention Centre at the garage at the municipal building in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that on the first floor was the police. In the garage was this temporary detention unit. And on the second floor was the Crisis Staff, or the council at the time, and later the Municipal Assembly, because we've already seen that the police station had been completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were aware of the status of Muslim detainees because you were a member of the municipal -- Serb Municipal Assembly of Hadzici, and issues relating to the detention of Muslim civilians was reported in sessions in which you participated; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, civilians were not detained in that garage, but people who violated the norms of the time, people who had weapons, who were shooting from the centre of town itself at, I don't know, certain facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, my question wasn't limited to the garage. My question was, and I'll repeat it: You were aware of the status of Muslim detainees because you were a member of the Serb Municipal Assembly in Hadzici and issues relating to the detention of Muslim civilians was reported in sessions in which you participated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated, but that was referred to very little at the sessions of the Crisis Staff. It was a body of a technical, coordinating nature, whereas what you're saying had to do with the police. No orders were issued to the police with regard to that, that is to say, arrests, bringing people into custody, seizing weapons, et cetera. That was done by the police itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did Muslim civilians remain in the sports complex for their own protection? When did they start to be detained and when did they stop being detained?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- well, I cannot say the exact date, but from the moment the conflict broke out, this tragic event that we've already spoken about -- or rather, not everybody stayed there for the same period of time. How should I put this? There was fluctuation through this building of these masses of people who were brought there; some were brought in, others were taken out. Now, were they exchanged? Some went back to their homes. But for the most part, I think - I'm not quite sure - but I think, say, by the beginning of August there were people in the sports centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from May to August people were in the sports centre, according to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people. I'm not saying that it's the same people who came on the 15th of May and stayed until the 10th of August. As far as I can remember, it is for that period of time that the centre was in existence, as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were being kept in the sports complex?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in conversation with a person who guarded the facility, it was approximately about 170 people who were in the building at a given point in time, but I could not give you the exact figure of the total number of people who went through the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In mid-June, your testimony this morning was that a group, a certain group, came in and ill-treated the Muslims. What was the name of that group?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very difficult time. Those things happened, unfortunately. A group came by. It appeared from no --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the group? Did it have a name, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't any organised group from any organised structure, either paramilitary or military, or police?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. As far as I can remember, and what people told me, they were half civilians, semi-civilians. That's the way I can put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified in respect of that particular incident that "we," referring to the Crisis Staff, "couldn't issue orders to the police because we had no authority over them." Who did have authority over the police?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had authority over the police, Mr. Banduka? If the Crisis Staff didn't, over the police, who had -- was it the minister of the interior --

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the then Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the way it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was responsible for the conditions that were in the sports centre?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a technical question. One could say that it was the Crisis Staff that was responsible, and then when the Assembly was established, the Assembly took over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't the situation this, Mr. Banduka: Muslim inhabitants of Hadzici were arrested in May, June, September, they were detained there not for their protection, oftentimes they were detained for purposes of use in exchanges, prisoner exchanges? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this was in view of protecting them, if that indeed had been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, would you please answer the questions. The question was not if there was an exchange, what was the reason for it. The question was, quite simply, is -- whether oftentimes they were detained for purposes of use in exchanges, prisoner exchanges; isn't that the case. I must, while rereading the question, I must admit, Mr. Harmon, that it was not clear to the extent that the purpose of their detention was mentioned. And of course, sometimes some matters can have more purposes. So let's first try to establish whether those who were detained, for whatever reason, whether they were part of exchange, of prisoners exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Many people who were in the sports hall were exchanged eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Banduka wasn't the reason they were arrested and put in the sports hall was for the purpose of using them for exchange?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that was the main reason, or the basic reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there were such cases. There probably were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to tab 14 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which has a number already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is -- tab 14 is P411.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, this is an intercepted communication between Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Mandic, and I'm going to read you a portion of it rather than have you read it. Mr. Mandic says, on the second page of the English, and you can follow along with me if you like. I'm starting reading on the second page of the B/C/S version, about a little bit past halfway down. Mr. Mandic, in this conversation, says: "Yes, yes, we're evacuating them." Karadzic: "How many will there be?" Mandic says: "Well, I don't really know. We have many on the list. There are 300 people from Hadzici, Muslims who have been kept here for seven days. No one's inquired about them. No one seems to care. I don't know what to do." Karadzic: "Why don't --" Mandic: "No one is interested in these Muslims." Karadzic: "Yeah." Mandic: "So we'll try to exchange them for these people from Hrasnica." Now, that talks about 300 Muslims being detained in Hadzici, and it talks about them being essentially used as possible exchange currency. What do you have to say about that, Mr. Banduka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first I have to tell you that the same situation was in Tarcin and that the news travel from one side to the other, as I have already told you, from one side to the other. The people who were in the sports hall all wanted to get to the Muslim territory. It was not possible to do that across the combat line. It was not possible to let people go and cross the defence line, because there was shooting going on. It is true that some of the people were transferred to Kula, which is mentioned in this conversation. I don't know how many of them, whether there were 300 of them. I can't remember. Or rather, I didn't know it. I don't know it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, again let me put a proposition to you, Mr. Banduka. Throughout the year of 1992, Bosnian Serbs in Hadzici continued to detain Muslim civilians for purposes of exchanging them; isn't that correct? They continued to arrest them and they continued to detain them, for no other reason than to use them for purposes of exchanging them and removing them from the municipality. Do you agree with that or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please explain what exchanges, why they had to be exchanged. If you're talking about exchanges, the Muslims on this side, what would we exchange them for, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, a majority of them were not arrested, were not detained. As I've already told you, they were put in this collection centre, they were provided with food, and some sort of living conditions, as well as protection from -- physical protection, because anything could have happened to them in those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could turn to tab 15. And this is not a document that is translated into B/C/S, but I can direct the witness in the English version quite easily to certain portions of it. Your Honour, this is a document that we received from the Alliance of Former Camp Inmates. It's data from that organisation, and it has --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Banduka, in the third column -- in the first column it has the name of the individual -- second column, I should say. In the third column it has the year and place of birth. In the fourth column it has the place of arrest. The next column it has the camp. The next column it has the time and date of arrival to the collection location, and the next column is the date of the departure. And then the rest of the data is not particularly important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in your tab 15, I'm sorry I forgot to mention there is a supplemental version. I'd ask Your Honours to disregard what is in tab 15, because there's a lengthier version that I was given during the recess, and if that could be distributed or has been distributed already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then that should be the version which should be the appropriate version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this, Mr. Banduka, this data that has been provided to us and is before you reflects that a number of Muslims were arrested throughout the period. The largest numbers of those people arrested were in May and in June and in September. So again I confront you with this document, Mr. Banduka, and again ask you if -- what your comments are in respect of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is at the very best second-hand hearsay. I would accept if the witness could deal with the names upon it, see if he knows of them, but I do invite the Court to -- invite the Prosecution to treat with the utmost caution a document which I say at the very best is second-hand hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My comment on this document, Your Honour, is it is of course hearsay. The reports and the data contained in it come from reports to the Alliance of Former Camp Inmates. The Court has heard testimony in respect of that organisation. And I'm putting to the witness this data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we could not ask the witness to read it. I don't know whether it is the purpose of the Prosecution to present this to the witness to see whether he recognises any names. But let's perhaps first ask the witness the following: You've got in front of you a list which is prepared by an organisation which seems to indicate on the basis of the time and date of arrival to collection, and, as you may see, that the camp is in a lot of records. It's the sports hall in Hadzici. Looking at the time of arrival, but also looking at the time and date of departure and from the collection, that it was in many cases far beyond the date you gave, at least as far as the time of departure is concerned. What would be your comment on this information, which seems to be quite different from the time-limit you indicated in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just spoke from memory, bearing in mind that I left for the army in the month of June, and the subsequent data is unknown to me. And this document is really not clear to me. Here you have the first name, the last name, and so on and so forth, and the persons who executed. What did they execute? What is this, who carried out something? What is that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which column are you referring to, Mr. Banduka, when you say "the persons who executed"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOMIR BANDUKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand. Here are the names of people. Are you saying that they were collected, that they were ... Here I only see the time of entering the camp and the time of leaving the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, may I take you to the fourth page from the bottom. I take it that the witness now has the version in front of him. You've got that, with at the bottom number 961?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you would look at the number just above that. That's 1201.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is about Djedovic Nermina. Is that the name of a female or of a male?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose, I assume, that this was a woman. How am I supposed to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it says that she was born in 1984 in Sarajevo, that she was arrested in Hadzici. The place of detention is sports centre Hadzici. And now I'm asking your specific attention for the next two entries, which is time and date of arrival to the collection. That's the 9th of September, and the time and date of departure from the collection is 27th of November. This is one example of what Mr. Harmon wants to confront you with, that is, that a list has been prepared by an organisation on which people appear to have been arrested after the time period you mentioned and were then detained for still a considerable period of time, which in this example would be two and a half months. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, this illustrates in my submission the problem with the document. Isn't there at least two different alleged places of detention in relation to 961?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And I therefore I fully understand your problem and it's certainly something that people come in and therefore I asked the attention of the witness -- you must have missed, first of all, the name I read out. I asked the witness to look at 1201.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not without a reason, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was for exactly the reason you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that I gave this as an example. So Mr. Harmon is confronting you now, with, for example, this person, who seems to be detained from mid-September until late November 1992 in the Hadzici sports centre and your testimony was that it was only until August that people were detained there. So the question is whether you can comment on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I thought that they had stayed there until August, but obviously, if this is a relevant piece of evidence, that I was mistaken. And I've also told you that I was in the army in July, and I told you that I spoke from memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, you felt free to say that it was until August, where you said you went to the army in July. And now your absence is used as an explanation why your information might be wrong. Wouldn't that be true then also for the second half of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have emphasised, in view of arriving at the truth, that I'm speaking from memory. Obviously I was not aware of the fact that this was a longer period of time. But if we were to analyse this document, I don't know how many such cases there were in the first place. That's why I don't want to say anything about those cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Harmon. I'm looking at the clock, and I get some outside warning as well, from what I see. I have one or two issues which first of all I take it you're not ready yet with your cross-examination, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No, I'm not. I was wondering if this could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1008, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. How much time would you still need, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would fit more or less, I think, in the 60 per cent guidance also. But I'll check that and I'll confirm to you whether there's still half an hour left, whether it would not be 20 minutes or 25 minutes or ... Then I would like to first of all instruct the witness not to speak with anyone about his testimony that you gave already and you're still about to give. We hope to finish with you tomorrow, but we're sitting in the afternoon and not in the morning. Hopefully we'll finish by the first break. So don't speak with anyone about your testimony, and I'll invite Madam Usher now to escort you out of the courtroom. Then I do understand that there is agreement on an application for protective measures which I don't remember to have seen yet, but it might be that it's there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was filed I think on Thursday, possibly Friday. It was certainly filed. I personally filed it on behalf of Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no problem and I do understand there's no objection against the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll deal with that. Then, Mr. Josse, the Davidovic submissions for due for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly the same. I filed them on behalf of both Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I asked our case manager to call OLAD. They've also been filed electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's great. Thank you very much. We will then adjourn until tomorrow afternoon in Courtroom II. And tomorrow afternoon is a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
